case_data.title: PAIR in Action: Co-Creating AI Inclusion with Financially Disadvantaged Communities
case_data.provide-a-brief-description-of-the-proje:
As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes everyday life, there is growing awareness that citizen participation in AI development and governance is essential. This is particularly critical for the most vulnerable communities – those least likely to be involved in participatory practices yet most likely to be impacted by AI systems (Oman & Cannizzaro, 2025).

This paper presents findings from participatory action research (PAR) workshops on AI inclusion, conducted with members of financially disadvantaged communities in the United Kingdom (UK). The central research question of the project is: how can we understand AI inclusion through dialogue with those experiencing financial disadvantage?

Over two series of workshops (4 workshops each), we engaged participants of mixed ages (including older adults) in Inverness (Scotland) and predominantly younger participants in London (England). Partnering with local charities, we co-created spaces to explore what AI means to these communities and identify the challenges and opportunities they perceive. Our methodological approach drew inspiration from 'Pedagogy of the Oppressed' (Freire, 1972), 'Teaching Community: A Pedagogy of Hope' (hooks, 2003), and Fals Borda’s (1987) ideas on participatory action research – demonstrating that methodologies originating in the Global South can be meaningfully applied in the Global North, learning from the experiences of the ‘South in the North’ (Medrado & Verdegem, 2024).

Our findings reveal that after sharing and discussing everyday life AI experiences (or the lack thereof), the participants developed nuanced understandings of the risks and benefits of AI. A critical aspect of participatory AI research with members of vulnerable communities is the barrier of inaccessible language around these technologies. Many participants faced literacy challenges, compelling us to reconsider how we discuss AI within these communities. This insight highlights the effectiveness of community teaching and learning, even when participants have limited knowledge and experience with AI.

The next phase of the project involves translating these co-created insights on AI inclusion into actionable proposals that can promote AI literacy, enabling participants to make informed decisions about whether and how to engage with AI, as well as the support they need. This research emphasises that genuine AI inclusion requires not only participatory research but also concrete pathways from dialogue to action – ensuring that the voices of financially-disadvantaged communities shape AI futures rather than simply being documented.

This work contributes to participatory AI research by centering marginalised voices, adapting Global South methodologies for Northern contexts, and identifying practical barriers to inclusion that must be addressed for equitable AI development.
